doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Pawning Peck Morrison's bass
summary: Strung out in 1959, Ware pawns a bass he took from a Brooklyn stage, which belonged to Peck Morrison.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And I started going around to different clubs; I went around to the Five Spot Firespot, and (unintelligible) and Jim Harlo, Hall, and who was there but Jimmy Giuffre, Jim and who was it that was on drums ... oh, the drummer, and Buell Neidlinger, Bill Nyad, a bassist that I knew; a white dude, that had been working mostly with Cecil Skeets Taylor. And they were good musicians.

And we were buddies. But I went in and I sat in with Giuffre for Dupree, and Giuffre Dupree wanted me to open up with him down at the Vanguard, and I didn't tell you this story, but back in the late fifties, '59, I hung strung out there in Harlem, and I come over to Brooklyn, and I had all my clothes and what not in this pawn shop, and I was going over there to get -- the guy knew me and all, I needed a few dollars, and I said, "Come on man, add some more on to the ticket, you know, and I'll come and get my stuff, you know," and he said, "No, I can't do that." Anyway, I wound up bad-off mad, and my sickness was coming down on me again, so I was walking passed this club, in the Club Baby Grand Brooklyn, and a guy with a fiddle was standing up on stage, and I just walked in there and took it out, took it down to the next block, and walked in there and took out my identification and pawned it for $50. And I said whoever's fiddle this is, they would know that I got it, and they know that I didn't try to sell it or nothing, so not to worry about it, you know. I had pawned it before, and once I pawn it, the word would

get around, and that person wouldn't kill me until they got their fiddle, you know. It turned out later that it was Peck Morrison's bass. But however, naturally, we had to report it to the police, and that's when they started looking for me. That was before I went to Chicago, and I'm not thinking about that so much, because I knew he got his fiddle the next day; he got it back, but the police was still looking for me for petit petty larceny. And it didn't come to the floor until I got back there in '60, and I played the Newport thing, and I was getting ready to join Jimmy Giuffre Jitfree (phonetic) and that's when the cabaret licenses were enforced then, and you had to have that cabaret license in order to work a nightclub.
